overview: The Wausau City Council held its regular meeting on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, taking up proclamations for Homelessness Awareness Month, Hmong New Year, and Veterans Day, then approving the 2027 City of Wausau budget on a 7-4 vote after rejecting an amendment to use reserves to achieve net-zero new borrowing. The council also unanimously approved the consent agenda, which included designating Yawkey Park as a local historic landmark, and passed several other resolutions including the 2027 comprehensive fee schedule and a police Beat Patrol grant acceptance under suspension of the rules.

discussions.body: Mayor Diny presented an update on the city administrator proposal, noting a public information session drew 45 residents and an ongoing resident survey had received 296 responses with a week remaining. He argued that a city administrator model—adoptable by simple ordinance—would provide continuity, professional management, and separation of politics from day-to-day operations, and asked the council to retain the $150,000 budget line for the position. Alder Tierney questioned the cost estimates, noting uncertainty in the figures, while Alder Hoenecke expressed skepticism that adding an administrator would tangibly address residents' concerns about spending and performance. Alder Neal called the $150,000 figure insufficiently supported and said the audit should come first; Alder Wiskowski asked that multiple models—including a chief-of-staff option—be presented at a future committee of the whole. No vote was taken; the mayor indicated a committee-of-the-whole session would follow.

discussions.item: Approval of Minutes from October 27 Regular Council Meeting
discussions.body: Alder Lukens requested a minor amendment to clarify that she had not objected but merely had a question during a prior item regarding the Flock camera resolution. A motion to amend was made by Lukens and seconded by Hoenecke; it passed on a voice vote. The amended minutes were then approved 11-0.

Four residents addressed the council. Two speakers focused on Flock license-plate-reader cameras, urging the council to send written termination notice to Flock by November 15 under contract Section 11.16, to omit Flock payments from the 2027 and 2028 budgets, and noting that 42 Wisconsin agencies had already ended or decided to end Flock contracts with no known litigation. One speaker read a statement from Yawkey heirs expressing full support for designating Yawkey Park as a historic landmark. A fourth speaker supported both the Yawkey Park landmarking and the city audit while expressing opposition to advancing a city administrator position without a referendum.

The consent agenda was moved by Neal and seconded by Slonski and passed unanimously 11-0. Mayor Diny specifically noted that the designation of Yawkey Park as a local historic landmark was included, calling out that it had passed unanimously through the Plan Commission and Historic Preservation Commission.

The budget came out of the Finance Committee 4-1. Alder Hoenecke moved an amendment to use general fund reserves to offset new borrowing so that net new debt would be zero (borrowing $18 million rather than $22 million); Finance Director Groat cautioned against it, noting Wausau's unassigned fund balance as a share of expenses was already on the lower end compared to peer cities, and recommended waiting until year-end. Alder Martens and Slonski also opposed the amendment, with Slonski citing the city's fund-balance policy limiting reserve draws to unanticipated, non-recurring needs; the amendment failed 2-9. On the main motion, Alder Wiskowski, Trueblood, and Lukens voiced concerns about the budget process, lack of broader public deliberation, and unresolved structural issues like a $1.368 million motor pool shortfall. Alder Martens, chair of Finance, summarized key amendments—reclassifying $150,000 from city administrator to audit, eliminating $50,000 for Flock, $45,000 for alley paving, $20,000 for trail planning, and $150,000 for downtown traffic redesign engineering—and noted 60% of the tax increase stems from fully funding 12 new firefighter-paramedics approved by April referendum. The budget was adopted 7-4, with an estimated $71.52 increase per $200,000 assessed home value.

discussions.item: Suspension of Rules and Beat Patrol Grant
discussions.body: The council voted 9-2 to suspend Rule 1D to allow late-arriving committee business. Under suspension, the council took up a Finance Committee resolution accepting a Wisconsin DOJ 2027 Beat Patrol Grant of $121,434 for the police department, which had passed Finance 5-0. Police Chief explained the grant has been received since 2019, is non-competitive but annual, and effectively funds approximately two officers; if lost, a difficult staffing conversation with the council would follow. Alder Hoenecke raised concern about vulnerability to federal funding changes and the lateness of the grant award relative to budget planning; the resolution passed 11-0.

A Finance Committee resolution approving the 2027 operating plan for Business Improvement District No. 1 downtown, which had passed Finance 5-0, was moved by Watson and seconded by Hoenecke. No discussion was recorded and it passed unanimously 11-0.

publicComment: Four residents spoke during public comment. Two speakers urged the council to send written termination notice to Flock Safety by November 15 under Section 11.16 of the contract, to exclude Flock payments from the 2027 and 2028 budgets, and noted no known litigation against any of the 42 Wisconsin agencies that had already ended Flock contracts. One speaker, the assistant director of the Leigh Yawkey Woodson Art Museum appearing in a professional capacity, read a statement from Yawkey heirs supporting designation of Yawkey Park as a historic landmark. A fourth resident, who identified herself as Christine Martins of Arthur Street, also spoke in support of the Yawkey Park landmarking and noted the letter from the Yawkey heirs had been read at every relevant meeting. A fifth resident (who spoke during the budget public hearing) expressed support for the audit over the city administrator proposal and said a survey was not sufficient substitute for a referendum on the administrator question.
